rounds.root_cause: The scorecard relies on a single holistic sentiment answer, and the errors fall into two repeatable families. First, mixed texts with a main clause plus a concession ('underwhelming... yet showed reasonable progress', 'encouraging... on the other hand areas needing work'): the holistic answer latches onto the concessive clause, while the human label consistently follows the main evaluative clause (and treats doubt/reservation as negative, and negated negatives like 'wasn't completely disorganized' as positive). Second, purely neutral procedural statements ('Review coordination is managed through the designated system') are always labeled negative, but the holistic answer reads their lack of negative words as positive. Decomposing sentiment into positive/negative presence, which side the main clause takes, and whether any evaluation exists at all gives the model the axes the label actually uses.

proposed.instructions: Does the text contain any positive evaluation of its subject (praise, approval, improvement, competence, or success), even if mild, hedged, or expressed by negating a negative (e.g., 'wasn't completely disorganized')?
Does the text contain any negative evaluation of its subject (criticism, disappointment, problems, or expressed doubt, reservations, or being conflicted), even if mild or hedged?

Identify the text's main evaluative claim, setting aside any concessive or qualifying clause introduced by words like 'yet', 'nevertheless', 'even so', 'though', 'while', or 'on the other hand'. Is that main claim positive or negative?
Is the text a purely factual or procedural statement (describing how something is managed, prepared, configured, or carried out) with no positive or negative evaluation anywhere in it?

rounds.root_cause: The scorecard relies on a single holistic sentiment answer, and the dominant error pattern is mixed two-clause sentences where the label consistently follows the FIRST evaluative clause (positive-then-caveat = positive, negative-then-reassurance = negative), while the holistic answer gets pulled by the second clause's strong opposite-valence words ('encouraging signs', 'reasonably aligned' vs 'questionable', 'inconsistent', 'shaky'). A secondary pattern is that hedged sports/leisure evaluations are labeled positive and hedged workplace evaluations negative even when surface wording points the other way, so domain context is also invisible to the current single feature.

proposed.instructions: If the text contrasts two evaluations (using words like but, though, however, yet, even so, although, on the other hand), what is the sentiment of the FIRST evaluation, before the contrast? If the text has only one evaluation, give its sentiment. If there is no evaluation at all, answer none.
What is the text mainly about: sports, exercise, or recreational activities; work, business, or organizational matters; or a neutral procedural or technical description with no evaluation?

rounds.root_cause: The label in this data is essentially the sentiment of the FIRST evaluation in the sentence: every contrast disagreement ('While the client call not quite, there were some encouraging signs' -> negative; 'golf practice seemed marginally more structured, though results were inconsistent' -> positive) follows the pre-contrast clause, and the primary_clause_sentiment element was built for exactly this. But its wording ('before the contrast') breaks on sentence-initial 'While/Although', where nothing precedes the contrast word, so the answering model systematically returns the SECOND (main) clause's sentiment -- the stored answers are inverted on exactly the items that decide the label. A secondary cluster of errors is terse procedural statements with no evaluation ('Email notifications were sent...', 'Personnel followed the updated protocols'), which the human labels negative while the model guesses positive; an explicit 'contains any evaluative judgment' check gives the model a handle on these.

proposed.instructions: Does the text express any evaluative judgment at all -- that something is good or bad, effective or ineffective, adequate or inadequate, successful or disappointing, even in hedged or negated form (e.g. 'not quite', 'wasn't completely disorganized', 'marginally better')? Answer no if the text only states that a routine action happened or a fact holds (e.g. notifications were sent, protocols were followed, materials were cataloged) with no judgment of how well or poorly anything is.

rounds.root_cause: The label in this data follows the FIRST evaluative judgment: hedged-negative openers ('not quite', 'doesn't fully', 'somewhat lacking', 'moderately concerning') map to negative even when a positive clause follows, and hedged-positive openers ('marginally better', 'partially successful', 'somewhat encouraging', 'not completely disappointing') map to positive even when a negative clause follows. primary_clause_sentiment is built for exactly this, but its answers are unreliable on these cases: when the opener's evaluative word is truncated ('the client call not quite') it answers 'positive' or 'none', and when the trailing clause has strong opposite words ('inconsistent', 'questionable', 'encouraging signs') it flips to the trailing polarity. A dedicated element that locks onto the polarity of the hedged/negated marker itself, with explicit instructions for incomplete judgments and for ignoring post-contrast clauses, attacks the large majority of the disagreements; contains_evaluation is near-useless (importance ~0.006) and its slot is better spent here.

proposed.instructions: Locate the FIRST hedged, negated, or qualified judgment in the text -- phrases like 'not quite', 'not entirely', 'doesn't fully', 'marginally below', 'somewhat lacking', 'moderately concerning', 'slightly underwhelming' (negative-leaning) or 'marginally better', 'marginally more structured', 'partially successful', 'somewhat encouraging', 'traces of improvement', 'not completely disappointing', 'wasn't completely disorganized' (positive-leaning). Judge the polarity of that phrase on its own: negations of good outcomes and shortfalls ('not quite', 'doesn't fully', 'not entirely', 'somewhat lacking') count as negative, while negations of bad outcomes and partial improvements ('not completely disappointing', 'partially successful', 'marginally better') count as positive. The phrase still counts even if its sentence is grammatically incomplete or the judged quality is left unstated (e.g. 'the client call not quite', 'our methodology doesn't fully'). Completely ignore any judgment that comes after a contrast word such as but, though, however, yet, even so, nevertheless, nonetheless, despite that, or on the other hand, and ignore purely procedural statements with no evaluative phrase. What is the polarity of that first hedged judgment?
